structured_output.hypothesis: If the cannon-bones of ox, sheep and giraffe differ essentially only by a one-axis stretch, then at equal length the sheep's metacarpal is about 2/3 and the giraffe's about 1/3 as broad as the ox's, and the three species share one shape beyond that length-to-breadth ratio.
structured_output.pass_criterion: Take the species-mean metacarpal (III+IV) greatest length L and mid-shaft mediolateral width W for Bos, Ovis and Giraffa. Define the slenderness ratio S = L/W. The claim passes if S_sheep/S_ox is between 1.35 and 1.65 (Thompson's 3/2 ±10%), AND S_giraffe/S_ox is between 2.7 and 3.3 (3 ±10%), which is the same as sheep breadth about 0.67 and giraffe breadth about 0.33 of the ox's at equal length. It must also pass a pure-stretch check: W/L is the same across the three species within 15% at every other measured position along the shaft, such as proximal and distal widths. If several ox, sheep or giraffe taxa are available, use the species-level means.
structured_output.fail_criterion: The claim fails if either ratio S_sheep/S_ox or S_giraffe/S_ox falls outside the bands above (sheep outside 1.35-1.65, giraffe outside 2.7-3.3), or if proximal, mid-shaft and distal width-to-length ratios do not scale by the same factor within 15%. In that case the bones differ in shape beyond a simple one-axis stretch.
structured_output.interpretation: Thompson's 'cannon-bone' is the metacarpus (fused metacarpal III+IV) of ruminants. 'Length' means the proximodistal greatest length. 'Breadth' means mediolateral width, and the 'simple stretch' is a uniform scaling of the vertical axis alone by a factor of 3/2 for sheep versus ox. His statement that the giraffe's bone is about one-third as broad at equal length is read as S_giraffe/S_ox of about 3. The modern reinterpretation uses species-mean linear measurements from museum skeletons, with Bos taken as Bos taurus or an equivalent bovine and Ovis as Ovis aries. A single mid-shaft width may not capture the whole outline, so I also test widths at the proximal and distal ends. Thompson drew from single illustrated specimens. A dataset with several measurements per species is a stricter test than his own comparison. I did not confirm that the file contains all three species or a mediolateral metacarpal width field. If any is missing, the test is undecidable with this dataset and I would report that instead of substituting another species.

dataset.name: Predicting body mass in Ruminantia using postcranial measurements
dataset.why_it_fits: The dataset covers 101 extant ruminant artiodactyl species and includes raw_postcranial_measurements.xlsx with 56 postcranial measurements. These include long-bone lengths and widths, and the README points to Table S3 for definitions. I would use the metacarpal length and the mediolateral width fields at proximal, mid-shaft and distal positions for Bos, Ovis and Giraffa, taking species means from body_mass_data.csv or the raw file. The page does not confirm that these species or a metacarpal breadth field are present, and checking that is the first step of the test.
